newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Row over NZ butter arrests in UK flares again.
newsitem.headline: Row over NZ butter arrests in UK flares again.

text.p: New Zealand said on Wednesday it would comply with a British customs request for help in its investigations into suspected quota fraud involving butter exports, but pledged to defend the key trade.
The request provoked anger from the New Zealand Dairy Board over the U.K. authorities' treatment of its six employees, who were arrested and charged with duty fraud in London 12 days ago.
The cooperative-run board believes they are being victimised as part of a wider campaign to cut its butter exports to Europe.
International Trade Minister Lockwood Smith said the top priority was to protect a trade worth an annual NZ$376 million ($260 million).
"I have instructed my officials to work with the Board to ensure that this trade is maintained," Smith said in a statement.

But he did not join the allegations of victimisation, saying only that his department was studying the case "to see if there are any broad trade policy issues involved that we need to discuss with the British authorities".
The butter trade with Europe, mainly under the Anchor brand, is controlled by strict European Union quota rules which Britain said the men had breached.
The New Zealand Attorney General's office confirmed it had been asked to cooperate with Britain's Customs and Excise under the terms of bilateral agreements and would be doing so.
"Assisting United Kingdom investigating authorities certainly involves no assumption as to guilt," it added.
An angry Dairy Board chairman, Sir Dryden Spring, called the latest request "totally unnecessary".
"We have been cooperating with British customs -- the board has nothing to hide. Every single request they have made we have complied with," he told Radio New Zealand.
"It is not necessary to go this extent to get the information they want," he added.
Dryden accused UK customs of being "aggressive and officious" with the charged executives, saying the heavy-handed approach was placing great strain on them and their families.
Smith said it had recently become clear that "differing views had emerged about provisions defining New Zealand's butter quota into Europe and its administration".
One example of this was the ongoing dispute, now with the World Trade Organisation, over New Zealand's right to include a new product known as spreadable butter in its European quota.
"If there are other problems that we need to resolve we will be happy to work through them with the (European) Commission," he added.
